case_study_insert.main_stem: Bluefern Safety Wear (BSW) is a partnership in the workwear manufacturing sector, producing high-visibility jackets, trousers and coveralls for rail, road and utility crews, with a workforce of 36. Founded in 2013 by Ramesh Kulkarni and Tolu Adeyemi, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. BSW plans to invest $620,000 in an automated cutting and reflective heat-sealing line, financed by a $350,000 five-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.20, and produces 72,000 units a year. BSW faces a 3.4% defect rate on heat-sealed seams and labour turnover of 14%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The heat-sealing line output 18,000 jackets last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 5.0% a year earlier, and rework fell 31%. Customer complaints dropped from 26 to 14 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.8 days. Market research of 350 contractor safety managers found that 61% would switch to garments made with recycled reflective tape, and 45% require EN-ISO certification on all orders. 9 of 36 machinists have not completed training on the new heat-sealer; off-the-job training at the textile college costs $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bluefern Safety Wear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.00 to $13.81 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for labour-intensive manufacturers. (3) Polyester and reflective-tape input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year and manufacturing input-cost inflation is running at 6.9%, while infrastructure spending on rail and road projects grew 4.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: BSW plans to finance part of its heat-sealing expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BSW of the bank loan instead of relying solely on retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bank loan gives BSW immediate access to a much larger sum than its retained profit position allows — $350,000 now rather than waiting years to accumulate profit — so the automated cutting and reflective heat-sealing line can be ordered and installed without delay. Every month of delay keeps BSW producing at a 3.4% defect rate while competitors improve; the loan converts future revenue into today's productive capacity.

Point 2: The loan leaves BSW's limited retained profit untouched as a safety buffer. BSW's 2025 balance sheet is tightening: inventories rose to $185,000 ahead of winter demand, trade receivables jumped to $150,000 and cash fell to $55,000. Relying solely on retained profit would empty the buffer exactly when contractors are paying late and current liabilities have reached $290,000. Fixed monthly repayments over five years are predictable, allowing Ramesh Kulkarni and Tolu Adeyemi to plan cash flow, while the interest is tax-deductible and far cheaper than losing the rail-contract supply window.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bluefern Safety Wear and its heat-sealing expansion.

questions.question_text: BSW is launching its new high-visibility range made with recycled reflective tape. Consider exhibiting at the National Rail Safety Expo, advertising in a safety-industry trade journal, or working with workplace-safety social media influencers. Which should BSW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National Rail Safety Expo: A two-day stand at the expo puts BSW directly in front of the rail and road contractor safety managers who already specify PPE, with live seam demonstrations showing the heat-sealed tape holding under flex testing. The cost of stand space, travel and samples would absorb a sizeable slice of the $620,000 expansion budget, and benefits arrive in one burst per year — but the enquiries gathered often convert into multi-year supply agreements, transformational for a 36-person partnership.

Trade journal advertising: Quarter-page adverts in a safety-industry journal, costing only a few thousand dollars per issue, reach certified buyers across the country, and suit BSW's EN-ISO certification story that 45% of safety managers require. However, print engagement is falling, response cannot be measured precisely, and the 61% of managers who would switch for recycled reflective tape may never see the message in time for their contract-renewal windows.

Workplace-safety social media influencers: Partnering with respected site-safety influencers to demonstrate the range on real infrastructure projects costs a fraction of the expo, speaks directly to the 61% of safety managers open to recycled tape, and delivers measurable views and enquiry clicks. Risks are inconsistent message control and a younger, more site-operative audience than procurement decision-makers.

Recommendation: BSW should choose the National Rail Safety Expo. In this contractor-specified safety-wear market, the sale is specified by named safety managers; face-to-face demonstration at the exact event where rail contractors renew PPE contracts is the fastest route to signed supply deals, justifying the higher cost against the $620,000 expansion. Trade journal advertising is rejected as too slow and unmeasurable for a launch; influencer marketing is rejected as aimed at the wrong audience (operatives, not specifiers). BSW should use social media influencers as a low-cost supplement rather than the lead channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BSW with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BSW with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the trade journal and influencers are rejected as lead channels.

questions.question_text: BSW operates a flat structure with democratic leadership and labour turnover of 14%. Explain two benefits for BSW of democratic leadership for its 36 machinists.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership in BSW's flat structure gives the 36 machinists a real voice in cutting schedules, seam standards and shift patterns, satisfying their esteem needs (Maslow) and building genuine commitment. Workers consulted on the new heat-sealing machine are more likely to spot seam defects early, driving the 3.4% defect rate further down and protecting BSW's EN-ISO certification that 45% of safety managers demand.

Point 2: Involvement generates practical ideas from the people handling every garment daily — for example on reflective-tape tension, press temperatures and waste off-cuts — improving quality and reducing the rework that already fell 31% after the new line was introduced. Higher commitment lowers the costly labour turnover of 14%, saving repeated recruitment and the $750 per-employee off-the-job training at the textile college, while democratic consultation preserves the informal, family-like culture that Ramesh Kulkarni and Tolu Adeyemi built when they founded BSW in 2013. Democratic practice also gives BSW early warning of trouble: round-table checks on the heat-sealing line surface seam defects within days, and involving machinists in setting rework budgets builds the ownership that keeps labour turnover from climbing past 14%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BSW's defect rate, turnover and expansion.

questions.question_text: BSW must train 9 machinists on the new heat-sealing machine. Consider on-the-job training on the production floor or off-the-job training at the textile college at $750 per employee. Which should BSW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the line is directly relevant to BSW's own sealers, tape types and defect standards; costs nothing in fees; keeps the 9 machinists productive; and fits the democratic culture by pairing them with experienced operators. Drawbacks are that line leaders are diverted from output, bad habits can pass from trainer to trainee, and there is no recognised certificate — a weakness because 45% of BSW's contractor customers demand EN-ISO documentation and formal training records.

Off-the-job training: The textile college course at $750 per employee costs $6,750 in total — easily affordable against a $620,000 expansion and a $350,000 loan. It gives structured, current skills, a recognised certificate for all 9 machinists, and removes them from the floor so quality instruction is undistracted. Drawbacks are lost production hours, travel and subsistence, and content that may not match BSW's exact machine settings, so on-site follow-up is still required.

Decision: BSW should choose off-the-job training at the textile college, followed by a short supervised on-the-job consolidation week. The certificate strengthens BSW's EN-ISO evidence pack for the 45% certification-dependent customers, and the cost is trivial next to the $620,000 line. Pure on-the-job training is rejected because unrecorded training weakens BSW's audit file and risks cementing the habits behind the 3.4% defect rate; pure classroom training without on-site follow-up is rejected because machine-specific settings would be lost. This blended route also signals investment in people, helping reverse 14% labour turnover. Ramesh Kulkarni and Tolu Adeyemi should review the outcome — the 3.4% defect rate and the EN-ISO audit results — at the next quarterly partners' meeting to confirm the blended approach is holding.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BSW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of on-the-job and off-the-job training in the context of BSW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of BSW with a well-justified decision covering cost, certification, disruption and skill relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BSW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $198,000 ÷ ($15.20 − $9.20) = $198,000 ÷ $6.00 = 33,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 33,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.20 − $9.20 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BSW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Management can compare the 33,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 72,000 units to confirm BSW is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 39,000 units, before approving phase two of the heat-sealing line.
2. A contribution per unit of $6.00 lets BSW model contractor discounts, for example a 5% price cut to $14.44 would cut contribution to $5.24, showing exactly how much extra volume the rail contracts must deliver to keep covering the $198,000 fixed costs.
3. Combining fixed costs of $198,000 with the $6.00 contribution helps managers verify whether the $350,000 five-year bank loan repayments can be met from operating cash flow, and to time future borrowing around the 6.2% minimum wage rise.
4. Unit cost data ($198,000 ÷ 72,000 units + $9.20 = $11.95) lets managers benchmark performance against the 14% labour turnover problem, target the 3.4% defect rate for reduction, and renegotiate the $9.20 variable cost with polyester and reflective-tape suppliers amid 9.8% input-cost inflation; labour productivity of 2,000 units per worker (72,000 ÷ 36) sets a realistic improvement target.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 33,000 units ($198,000 ÷ $6.00) | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 ($15.20 − $9.20) | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 39,000 units against 72,000-unit output; contractor discount modelling on the $15.20 price against $198,000 fixed costs; feasibility check for the $350,000 five-year bank loan financing the $620,000 heat-sealing line; unit-cost benchmarking at $11.95 and labour productivity of 2,000 units per worker (72,000 ÷ 36) to target the 3.4% defect rate and the 14% labour turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BSW's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BSW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.62 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.34 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.71 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $80,000 cash = $315,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $150,000 + $55,000 = $390,000. 2024: $315,000 ÷ $195,000 = 1.62; 2025: $390,000 ÷ $290,000 = 1.34. For the stricter measure, 2024: ($315,000 − $140,000) ÷ $195,000 = $175,000 ÷ $195,000 = 0.90; 2025: ($390,000 − $185,000) ÷ $290,000 = $205,000 ÷ $290,000 = 0.71.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated, not improved. Although current assets rose by $75,000, current liabilities rose far faster, from $195,000 to $290,000, so both coverage measures fell. The deterioration is partly inventory-led: inventories climbed from $140,000 to $185,000 ahead of expected winter infrastructure orders, yet cash fell from $80,000 to $55,000. Most worryingly, trade receivables jumped from $95,000 to $150,000 — a large rail contractor is paying late — and the acid test now stands at only 0.71, meaning BSW cannot meet short-term debts without selling stock. With a $350,000 bank loan serviced monthly, this is a warning sign.

Conclusion: BSW's financial position has not improved. Liquidity weakened on both measures and the quality of current assets declined, with rising stock and slow-paying receivables masking the asset growth. BSW must tighten credit terms for rail contractors, agree staged payments on the winter order book, and review the reorder level before the next bank loan instalment — otherwise the $620,000 expansion risks a cash-flow crisis.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion that BSW's financial position has not improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BSW of making its high-visibility range from recycled reflective tape and fabric.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled-polyester fabric and tape align directly with the 61% of surveyed contractor safety managers who would switch suppliers for exactly this feature, letting BSW win EN-ISO-sensitive contracts and charge a small premium that protects its $6.00 contribution per unit even as polyester input costs rise 9.8%. It also strengthens BSW's brand with the 45% of buyers who require certified traceability documentation, helping convert the $620,000 heat-sealing line into multi-year rail and road contracts.

Disadvantage: Recycled materials typically cost more than virgin polyester, squeezing the $9.20 variable cost and the $6.00 contribution unless the premium is accepted by contractors — and BSW's trade receivables are already stretched, so a price increase could slow payment further. Supply risk is also real: recycled tape volumes are less predictable, and any inconsistency in recycled fibre quality would raise the 3.4% defect rate and the 14% labour turnover burden through re-cut seams and rework.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BSW's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in polyester and reflective-tape input costs will affect BSW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise to 5.25%: BSW's $350,000 five-year bank loan, if variable-rate, costs about $2,600 extra interest a year (0.75% of the balance) — a manageable sum, though BSW's already-thin $55,000 cash reserve and the $290,000 current liabilities make any additional expense uncomfortable, and higher rates could put some contractor customers' own projects on hold.

Minimum wage increase of 6.2% to $13.81: BSW's 36 sewing, cutting and packing staff are the heart of the business. If average earnings are near $13.81 an hour for 2,080 hours, each worker adds about $1,676 a year, or around $60,300 across the workforce — a serious hit against $198,000 of fixed costs, though productivity of 2,000 units per worker and the new automated cutting line can offset part of it through less overtime and reduced rework.

Input cost inflation of 9.8% (polyester and reflective tape): BSW's $9.20 variable cost is material-heavy; a 9.8% rise on the fabric and tape component (roughly $5.50-$6.00 of the unit cost) adds about $0.54-$0.59 per garment. Across 72,000 units that is roughly $39,000-$42,000 a year, trimming contribution per unit from $6.00 toward $5.40-$5.50 and narrowing the margin that supports the $620,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. BSW is labour-intensive — cutting, sewing and hand-finishing hi-vis — so the ~$60,300 wage-bill rise exceeds the ~$39,000-$42,000 input-cost impact and dwarfs the ~$2,600 interest-rate effect, and it cannot be avoided by redesigning the garment. BSW should respond by accelerating the cutting automation that is the core of the $620,000 expansion, tightening overtime, and renegotiating contractor rates upward in line with the 4.1% growth in infrastructure spending.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BSW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BSW's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BSW with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
